item.title: How New York City Homebuyers Can Use a Commission Rebate Strategically in 2026
item.dc:creator: Mike Mishkin
item.description:
Buying an apartment in New York is a balancing act. You want a home in a neighborhood you love, but you need to make sure

The post How New York City Homebuyers Can Use a Commission Rebate Strategically in 2026 appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.
item.content:encoded:
Buying an apartment in New York is a balancing act. You want a home in a neighborhood you love, but you need to make sure the numbers work for your current budget and your long-term plans. Even when you have plenty of cash to spend, there are ways to structure a purchase strategically, reducing your effective acquisition cost and creating additional room in your budget.

One way is through a buyer commission rebate. The way a buyer rebate works is simple: your agent returns a portion of the commission they receive for representing you. Prevu offers eligible New York buyers up to 1.5% of the purchase price back through its Smart Buyer Rebate Program, with the specific rebate disclosed before an offer is made. For a $2 million apartment, that could mean up to $30,000 back. That money can then become part of your purchasing strategy, whether you’re budgeting for renovations, evaluating a new development, or competing for a dream apartment at the upper end of your budget.

Here are three ways NYC buyers can use a rebate as part of their purchasing strategy.

Put the rebate toward a renovation

Apartments that need updating can offer opportunities for buyers who are prepared to take on the work. A dated kitchen or bathroom or other deferred improvements may mean you have room to negotiate on the purchase price. The rebate you receive can then help offset some of the cash required for improvements and work. Instead of viewing renovation costs separately from the purchase, consider the combined economics of the negotiated price, expected renovation budget, and your rebate.

This strategy can be particularly relevant on the Upper West Side, where many prewar apartments may need modernization. As Sara Gladstone, a Prevu real estate advisor, explains: “On the Upper West Side, some of the best opportunities I’ve found for buyers are in well-located prewar apartments that need updating, where negotiating for condition and layering in a buyer rebate can create meaningful value.”

Before making an offer, buyers should consider likely renovation costs and use recent comparable sales to determine how the property’s condition could factor into negotiations. 

Pair the rebate with new-development incentives

Searching for a condo in a new development gives buyers another opportunity to get more value from their budget. Sponsors, typically the lead developer of a property, may offer concessions such as paying transfer taxes, covering certain closing costs, or providing credits toward common charges. These incentives can often be negotiated, especially when sponsors want to move inventory, and should be considered alongside the purchase price when comparing units.

A buyer rebate can stack with these concessions, providing an additional source of savings and reducing the overall cost of the transaction without requiring the sponsor to reduce the unit’s asking price. When evaluating a new development, consider the purchase price, sponsor concessions, closing costs, and potential rebate together to understand the full economics of the purchase.

Use the rebate when competing for your dream apartment

A buyer rebate can also matter when an apartment attracts multiple offers. Competitive situations often require buyers to decide how much they are willing to spend to secure a property they want. A rebate can reduce your effective acquisition cost, creating additional room within your overall budget.

For example, a buyer who expects to receive $30,000 back on a $2 million purchase can factor that potential savings into the total cost of acquiring the apartment. The rebate does not change the seller’s proceeds, but it can affect the buyer’s net cost after closing.

This strategy can be particularly useful when something about the apartment cannot be replicated elsewhere. If a property has the location, layout, light, or other characteristics you’ve been searching for, a rebate can become part of the strategy you use to pursue it.

Make the Math Work for Your Move

A buyer rebate can do more than simply reduce your closing costs. Used strategically, it can become part of how you evaluate properties, structure offers, and allocate your purchasing budget.

Whether you’re considering a co-op that needs work, evaluating incentives on a new development, or competing for a highly desirable home, understanding your potential rebate can help you assess the full economics of the transaction.

Ready to buy in NYC? Browse listings and see how much you could save with Prevu’s Smart Buyer commission rebate.

item.title: Police Ask for Help Finding Missing Upper West Side Teen
item.dc:creator: Mike Mishkin
item.description:
Police are asking for the public's help finding a missing 17-year-old.

The post Police Ask for Help Finding Missing Upper West Side Teen appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.
item.content:encoded:
Police are asking the public for help finding a 17-year-old girl who has gone missing from the Upper West Side.

Amber Bell, who lives at 216 West 63rd Street, was last seen at her home on Wednesday, August 12, at around 4 p.m., according to the police report.

She’s described as a Black female, about 5 feet 4 inches tall and 140 pounds. She was last seen wearing a white tank top, gray sweatpants, and white sneakers.

Anyone with relevant information is asked to call the NYPD’s Crime Stoppers Hotline at 1-800-577-TIPS (8477) or for Spanish, 1-888-57-PISTA (74782). The public can also submit their tips by logging onto the Crime Stoppers website or by sending a direct message to @NYPDTips on Twitter. All calls are strictly confidential.

item.title: Human-Forward Tutoring for the AI Age
item.dc:creator: Joel Meyers and Gabe Matos
item.description:
Careful, there’s a ghost in this article: it’s your student’s living, breathing tutor. Or at least that’s how the AI overlords might introduce us, as

The post Human-Forward Tutoring for the AI Age appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.
item.content:encoded:
Gabe Matos and Joel Meyers are the founders of Hyperspace Tutors

Careful, there’s a ghost in this article: it’s your student’s living, breathing tutor.

Or at least that’s how the AI overlords might introduce us, as stewards of a bygone era of education. Why hire a tutor when the infinite encyclopedia of the internet can now personally lecture students on any subject at any time with no more than a prompt?

The question we’re asking at Hyperspace Tutors, however, is a little different. In fact, it’s the same question we’ve been asking from the start: given the marvels of information technology, where do today’s students still need support?

Hi, we’re Gabe and Joel, two Columbia grads who met puzzling over physics problems in the lounge of our freshman dorm. Whether volunteering to teach early math literacy, designing online courses for high school students, or swapping notes on our early tutoring endeavors, we became fast friends through a shared passion for helping others love learning as much as we do.

When we started Hyperspace on the wings of the COVID pandemic and our livestreamed graduation, Zoom-weary students needed a reason to love learning again. We quickly found that the technology wasn’t the problem: video conferencing makes education more accessible than ever, but students need a reason to turn on their cameras and unmute their microphones.

We made it our mission, then, to meet students at their interests first and build their learning experience around the things they actually care about. Soccer player cramming for a trigonometry test next week? Let’s talk about how triangles can get you all the way down the pitch. Dancer dreading that next physics quiz? Let’s think about how the mechanics of rotational inertia can help you sail through your next pirouette. To this day, we hand-select our tutors not only for their expertise, but also their commitment to connecting with students through shared interests. With that personal touch that tutoring affords, remote learning becomes an engaging expansion – rather than a dull extension – of the classroom.

Five years later, we’re asking the same question with the rise of ChatGPT and other LLM chatbots: where can we support students who have access to a digital Socrates in their pocket?

It is already clear that students need help navigating how – and when – to use AI at all. If the recent restrictions that NYC schools have placed on generative AI in the classroom are any indication, schools are struggling to help students decide between use cases that help and hinder their learning. Without careful prompting, LLMs spit out walls of text that can lose student attention even faster than a textbook. Worse, without clear, well-prompted guardrails, LLMs are quick to auto-complete entire assignments rather than guide a student to their own understanding. We do students the greatest disservice when we leave them to discern between truth and hallucination from a chatbot that presents every “fact” with unwavering professorial confidence. LLMs may be an inevitable learning tool of the future – look no further than Khan Academy Founder Sal Khan’s book Brave New Words for a convincingly optimistic prediction of AI’s potential to revolutionize education – but used indiscriminately, they threaten to replace critical thinking when they should be empowering students to take their thinking further.

Having long balanced the line between homework help and homework replacement, AI-literate tutors are uniquely positioned to help students navigate chatbot use with more nuance than a classroom curriculum allows. As subject experts, we can turn hallucinations from a pitfall into a learning opportunity on the age-old importance of healthy academic skepticism. Better yet, through one-on-one guidance, we can help students develop prompting habits that direct chatbots to support rather than supplant their personal learning style by restricting output length, citing real sources, or even withholding answers in favor of a more Socratic, step-by-step approach. Successful students in the AI age will be the ones who make sure they are the ones prompting the LLMs, not the other way around.

As tutors, we can also help students develop a healthy ethics around AI. LLMs are incredibly efficient, but efficiency is an opportunity, not an obligation. It is important that students learn there is still value in taking the time to struggle through an assignment, even when you could prompt it away in a second. Why turn to a bullet-point summary of the Gettysburg Address when you can feel proud having spent the time to pick apart the primary source yourself? Why not pat yourself on the back for taking the extra 20 minutes to wrestle through the last step of a tricky integral instead of prompting the explanation? It’s hard for a student who already feels stuck in their learning to see the reward on the other side of effort, and AI only makes matters worse by enticing students to kick the can down the road. Sometimes, the only way out is through, and that’s where a trusted mentor who can guide, empathize, and uplift is poised to help a student appreciate the value in making their own accomplishments.

Looking toward the long-term, human tutors also offer a unique arena in which students can rehearse the interpersonal and communication skills that will be essential in a post-generative workforce re-shaped by AI. For better or worse, proficiencies in copywriting and coding aren’t likely to stand out on future resumes. Rather, employers will hire for the ability to organize, communicate, and delegate high-level strategy; the more that AI takes over the work on our screens, the more we as professionals will have to look up to engage with and motivate the other humans (and bots) around us.

A live tutoring session is a private training ground for these kinds of interpersonal skills. Social media already lures students toward the “safety” of the screen, and it’s no shock that studies already report that students find human tutors more intimidating at first glance than our programmatically cheery counterparts. The stakes of human interaction, though, are a feature, not a bug. The same studies find that by pushing students to express and defend their thoughts on the spot – not to mention navigating the nerves and emotions that bubble up in the process – human tutors are much more effective at teaching students to calibrate toward an emotional common ground with their audience over time. In other words, the longer a student works with a human tutor, the more confident and comfortable they become in communicating their ideas face-to-face. In a mediascape that constantly tries to pull our attention away from one another, any opportunity that helps students develop their facility for face-to-face interaction will give them a leg up in whatever field they choose to pursue.

None of which is to say that our approach as tutors won’t, or shouldn’t, change. Gone, likely, are the days when it was enough to stroll up with a custom sheet of practice problems. ChatGPT can make a hundred such sheets in a fraction of the time, and probably with more depth and breadth (given a well-oiled prompt, of course). Even personal study plans, while they may benefit from the accountability of a live tutor, are easy to generate for any subject and learning style. Instead, we may better serve our students as academic coaches: always there to answer lingering questions (we’re still nerds, after all), but also stewards for helping each student discover and commit to their own ethics – and joy – of learning.

So, to answer our own question, yes: even with AI, we still see opportunity for real tutors to support real students. As long as students and families continue to seek that support, we won’t be closing up shop at Hyperspace anytime soon.

If you or a student you know could use our help navigating the AI age, we’d love to work with you.

Hyperspace Tutors is an NYC-based tutoring service that serves middle, high school, and undergraduate students nationwide in all areas of Mathematics, Humanities, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Test Prep (SAT, ACT, ISEE, SHSAT), College Essay Writing, and more.  Learn more and reach out at www.hyperspacetutors.com.

Gabe Matos is a PhD candidate in Physics at Columbia University, currently working on the CERN particle collider in Geneva, Switzerland.

Though he’s left Physics to Gabe for now, Joel Meyers hopes to play a real scientist on TV one day.  He came closest most recently as Albus Potter in Broadway’s Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.

item.title: Spirit Halloween Is Opening at a New Upper West Side Location
item.dc:creator: Mike Mishkin
item.description:
Upper West Siders hunting for a Halloween costume may not have to travel far this year. Spirit Halloween is opening a store in the neighborhood,

The post Spirit Halloween Is Opening at a New Upper West Side Location appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.
item.content:encoded:
Photo by @mikemcgue

Upper West Siders hunting for a Halloween costume may not have to travel far this year. Spirit Halloween is opening a store in the neighborhood, and it’s moving into a space once occupied by a familiar drugstore chain.

Advertisement

The new store is coming to 1889 Broadway (between 62nd and 63rd streets), which was previously home to a Duane Reade.

It won’t be the neighborhood’s first Spirit Halloween. A pop-up moved into the former Ricky’s at 112 West 72nd Street after that store closed, as I Love the Upper West Side reported at the time.

As for when it’ll open, that’s still up in the air. A Spirit Halloween spokesperson couldn’t give I Love the Upper West Side an exact date and referred us to the location page to check for updates.

Spirit Halloween stores sell costumes for adults, kids and pets, along with indoor and outdoor decorations and animatronic figures, which the company says get new releases each year. Much of the merchandise is officially licensed, and the company’s New York page name-checks franchises like Spider-Man, Harry Potter, Terrifier, Lilo & Stitch, Five Nights at Freddy’s and SpongeBob SquarePants. Spirit describes its stores as immersive Halloween destinations, complete with larger-than-life displays and jump scares.

Spirit Halloween has more than 1,500 stores across the U.S. and Canada and bills itself as the largest Halloween retailer in North America.

item.title: Police Seek Suspect in 11 Robberies in One Week, Including on the Upper West Side
item.dc:creator: Mike Mishkin
item.description:
The NYPD is asking the public for help identifying the suspect.

The post Police Seek Suspect in 11 Robberies in One Week, Including on the Upper West Side appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.
item.content:encoded:
The NYPD is asking for the public’s help identifying an individual wanted in connection with 11 robberies across the city in about a week, some of which happened on the Upper West Side.

Advertisement

According to the police report, the suspect approached victims while on a moped, displayed a knife and forcibly took money, jewelry and cellphones. All 11 incidents happened between Wednesday, Aug. 19 and Wednesday, Aug. 26.

The robberies took place within seven precincts. On the Upper West Side, that includes the 20th Precinct, which covers the neighborhood’s southern half, and the 24th Precinct, which covers its northern half. The others took place within the 1st Precinct (Financial District, Tribeca, Battery Park City and part of SoHo), the 6th Precinct (Greenwich Village and the West Village), the 10th Precinct (Chelsea and Hudson Yards), the 18th Precinct (Midtown West, including Hell’s Kitchen and Times Square) and the 94th Precinct (Greenpoint, Brooklyn). The report doesn’t say how many of the robberies happened in each precinct or give specific locations.

The rest of the draft stays the same.

Police have released these surveillance images of the suspect:

Anyone with relevant information is asked to call the NYPD’s Crime Stoppers Hotline at 1-800-577-TIPS (8477) or for Spanish, 1-888-57-PISTA (74782). The public can also submit their tips by logging onto the Crime Stoppers website or by sending a direct message to @NYPDTips on Twitter.

item.title: Father of Two Dies Days After Being Struck by Cyclist in Central Park
item.dc:creator: Mike Mishkin
item.description:
He was hit while walking to work last week.

The post Father of Two Dies Days After Being Struck by Cyclist in Central Park appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.
item.content:encoded:
via GoFundMe campaign

A 41-year-old man who was hit by a cyclist while walking to work through Central Park last week has died, and a fundraiser for his wife and two young daughters has already drawn about 1,500 donations.

Advertisement

Richie O’Brien, a union steamfitter from Port Jefferson Station in Long Island, died early Sunday, September 27, four days after the crash, according to the family’s GoFundMe. Police were called to the scene around 6:36 a.m. on Wednesday, September 23, according to the police report. A 32-year-old man was riding a bicycle northbound on West Drive while O’Brien was walking in the roadway, and the cyclist struck him. O’Brien fell to the ground and suffered severe head trauma. The cyclist was also thrown from the bike and had minor injuries.

Police haven’t released the cyclist’s name, and no arrests have been made. The NYPD’s Collision Investigation Squad is investigating.

O’Brien was taken to NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center and placed in a medically induced coma, his aunt, Luann Moskowitz, said in Instagram posts first reported by Our Town. She said he’d had two brain surgeries, and that it took EMS 15 minutes to reach him because of congestion from the United Nations General Assembly.

The police report places the crash on East Drive near East 84th Street.

“We are incredibly grateful for the love, prayers, and support that have surrounded Richie and his family throughout this heartbreaking journey,” the family said in a statement. In an update on the fundraiser, organizer Casey Bartels wrote that O’Brien died with his wife by his side and was able to donate his organs.

O’Brien is survived by his wife, Ronni, and their daughters, Kylie and Mia, who are 8 and 12. According to the fundraiser, Ronni has been a stay-at-home mom, and the money will go toward immediate expenses and their mortgage. As of writing, it has raised more than $177,000 of its $200,000 goal. Anyone who wants to contribute can do so here.

Advertisement

The Central Park Conservancy renewed its call last week for more safety measures on the park’s drives, including a 15-mph speed limit that the city’s Department of Transportation put in place but that’s now suspended amid litigation. The group is also pushing for stronger enforcement and better bike infrastructure around the park’s perimeter so commuters and delivery riders don’t have to cut through the park.

The City Council is scheduled to take up more than a dozen bills related to micromobility on Wednesday, according to Streetsblog.

item.title: Velvet Cowboy, a Western Bar With a $5 Food Menu, Opens on the Upper West Side Tomorrow
item.dc:creator: Mike Mishkin
item.description:
The Jacob's Pickles team's new bar opens Tuesday with Southwest-inspired cocktails and a menu where every dish costs $5.

The post Velvet Cowboy, a Western Bar With a $5 Food Menu, Opens on the Upper West Side Tomorrow appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.
item.content:encoded:
c/o Velvet Cowboy

Velvet Cowboy, a new bar from the team behind Jacob’s Pickles, opens on the Upper West Side on Tuesday, with a concept inspired by the American Southwest and the 1970s.

Advertisement

The bar is at 509 Amsterdam Avenue (between 84th and 85th streets), in the longtime home of Jacob’s Pickles. Jacob’s Pickles has since moved to a much larger space at 680 Columbus Avenue (between 93rd and 94th streets). Both are run by Jacob Hadjigeorgis’s Pickle Hospitality Group.

The bar pays homage to desert landscapes, roadside bars, old motels and vintage Americana, according to its Resy listing. “Dust off your boots, grab your favorite partner, and get ready to throw back a few, and ride ’till the sun comes up!” the bar wrote when it announced the opening.

The cocktail menu has riffs on classics like the Margarita and Boulevardier, plus original drinks. Every food item costs $5, and the dishes are meant for sharing. The Infatuation notes that the drinks include a julep made with sassafras and an absinthe drink called the Dead Man Walking. It also reported that the food includes Texas chili, Frito pie, and the bar’s own take on a McRib.

The first available reservations are for Thursday, Oct. 1, and they’re only for the cocktail lounge in the back. “Seats are limited so we ask that all reservations enjoy a 90 minute experience,” the listing reads. “Want to keep the rodeo going? Our front saloon is always open for walk ins and [is] the perfect place to grab your next cocktail!” After 6 p.m., everyone entering has to be 21 or older with a valid ID.

Hadjigeorgis founded Pickle Hospitality Group in 2011 with Jacob’s Pickles. The group later added Maison Pickle and Tiki Chick, as well as Lucky Pickle Dumpling Co., though that one closed in 2021.

item.title: Talea Beer Co. Opens Upper West Side Taproom in a Beloved Irish Bar’s Old Space
item.dc:creator: Mike Mishkin
item.description:
A woman-owned brewery has just moved into a familiar Upper West Side corner.

The post Talea Beer Co. Opens Upper West Side Taproom in a Beloved Irish Bar’s Old Space appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.
item.content:encoded:
Photo by @fleker

Talea Beer Co., the woman-owned brewery with taprooms across Brooklyn and Manhattan, opened its doors on the Upper West Side last week, and it’s moved into a corner space that plenty of neighbors will remember well.

Advertisement

The new taproom is at 441 Amsterdam Avenue on the corner of West 81st Street, the former home of St. James Gate. The Irish bar and restaurant, which opened in 2007, held its final night on Dec. 18, 2024. Employees and regulars told ILTUWS at the time that ballooning rent was behind the closing.

Talea was founded by Tara Hankinson and LeAnn Darland, who serve as the company’s co-CEOs. Every Talea beer is brewed at its flagship brewery and taproom in Williamsburg, which opened in March 2021, and the company also runs locations in Cobble Hill, the West Village, Bryant Park and near Penn Station. As a farm brewery, Talea uses a proportion of New York State ingredients.

The Upper West Side bar serves beer, wine, cocktails, coffee and non-alcoholic options. The food menu includes Detroit-style sourdough pizzas and Bavarian pretzels, along with salads, toasts, cheese plates and snacks.

Hankinson and Darland met while working at Hopsy, a beer e-commerce startup, after leaving jobs at The New York Times and Google. According to the company, they shared a frustration with the way craft beer was marketed to women and wanted to build an inclusive, approachable beer company. They filed the paperwork to form Talea three months after meeting.

Talea says its beers are known for fruit-forward flavors and playful takes on classic styles, and they’re sold at more than 1,300 retailers, bars and restaurants across New York State. The company also says it always keeps non-alcoholic options on the menu and puts changing stations in its bathrooms.

item.title: The JCC Has Volunteer Opportunities for Upper West Siders Who Can Spare 50 Minutes a Week
item.dc:creator: Mike Mishkin
item.description:
The Marlene Meyerson JCC Manhattan has lined up a slate of fall volunteer opportunities, and one of them puts you inside a neighborhood public school.

The post The JCC Has Volunteer Opportunities for Upper West Siders Who Can Spare 50 Minutes a Week appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.
item.content:encoded:
The Marlene Meyerson JCC Manhattan has a full slate of volunteer opportunities lined up for this fall, and the barrier to entry is lower than you might expect. Several ask for as little as one session a week, none of them require leaving the neighborhood, and one of them comes with training. One will put you inside a local public school, two others take place a couple of blocks apart on West 86th Street, and the fourth involves an election.

The school-based option is the JCC’s volunteer tutoring program, run through its Koopersmith Family Literacy + Math Program, which places volunteers in Upper West Side public schools for the 2026–27 school year. For most programs, the JCC asks every tutor to commit to at least one session per week and to show up consistently, since, as it puts it, consistency is crucial for the elementary school kids it serves. For the Reading to the Tinies program, volunteers can commit to as little as one 30-minute read-aloud session per semester. Tutors don’t replace certified teachers, but they’re trained for the role, and the JCC holds regular workshops where volunteers can pick up new skills and swap ideas with one another. Anyone with prior tutoring or teaching experience can flag it on the registration form and may be tapped for leadership opportunities.

The daytime roles all run Monday through Thursday during school hours:

  • Twice Weekly Literacy Tutoring at PS 145 (150 W 105th St): one-on-one work with a student in grades 1–2, two 50-minute sessions a week between 8 a.m. and 2:30 p.m., using structured lesson plans. Volunteers also attend four literacy training sessions over the year. The JCC calls it ideal for someone who wants a more intensive approach.
  • Reading Buddies at PS 163 (163 W 97th St) and PS 84 (32 W 92nd St): read with struggling students in grades 1–5 during lunch and recess, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., one 50-minute session a week.
  • General Classroom Assistance at PS 145 and PS 87 (160 W 78th St): flexible support for teachers and students in general education classrooms, one 50-minute session a week between 8 a.m. and 2:30 p.m. Space is limited, and it’s best suited for people with prior classroom experience.
  • Library Assistance at PS 145: one shift a week, Tuesday through Friday, 9–11 a.m. or 1–2:30 p.m., helping with storytime, read-alouds, crafts, shelving, cataloging, or tech in the school’s new library.

There are after-school options too:

  • English Language Learners After School Support: help ELL students in grades K–5 with academic and language development, Monday through Thursday, 3–4:30 p.m., one afternoon a week.
  • West Side Y + JCC (5 W 63rd St): read aloud to pre-K students, Monday through Thursday, 3:45–4:15 p.m. Background clearance for this one is handled separately by the West Side Y.

Session times are set to match the schools’ schedules, so the JCC can’t accommodate tutoring outside those hours. You can register to volunteer for the school year through the JCC’s sign-up form.

If a weekly commitment isn’t in the cards, the JCC also runs one-off shifts with two neighborhood organizations. The first is a food-packing shift at West Side Campaign Against Hunger, one of the largest emergency food providers in New York, at its site at 86th Street and Broadway. Volunteers assemble bags of fresh and shelf-stable food for food-insecure New Yorkers, restock the packing tables, break down boxes, and help with cleanup. Shifts run on select Tuesday mornings from 8:45 to 11 a.m. through November, and they’re open to all ages, though you should be comfortable standing for the whole time. First-time volunteers have to create an account on WSCAH’s Volunteer Hub and sign a waiver before showing up.

The second is a clothing-sorting shift at St. Paul and St. Andrew United Methodist Church (263 W 86th St at West End Ave), where volunteers accept, organize, and display donated items for a free distribution event for new immigrants held the following day. Shifts run on select Sunday afternoons from 1 to 3 p.m. through early December. It’s open to all ages, and children under 16 must be accompanied.

And then there’s the election. The JCC is running a nonpartisan Get Out the Vote effort ahead of the November general election, and it needs volunteers to help engage and inform neighbors about voting deadlines and early voting. Two-hour shifts take place at the JCC (334 Amsterdam Ave at 76th St) on select weekdays starting Sept. 22 and running right up through Election Day on Nov. 3, with morning and afternoon slots available. Volunteers of all backgrounds are welcome.

If you’d rather brush up on the basics first, the JCC’s Vote NY 2026 page has registration deadlines, early voting dates, and a polling-site lookup.

Questions about registering for any of the volunteer projects can go to the JCC at boxoffice@mmjccm.org.

The post The JCC Has Volunteer Opportunities for Upper West Siders Who Can Spare 50 Minutes a Week appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.

item.title: Café des Artistes Is Returning, and Anyone Who Ever Ate There Can Help Shape It
item.dc:creator: Mike Mishkin
item.description:
A restaurant that fed the Upper West Side for more than 90 years is making a comeback, and the team behind it is asking New Yorkers to pitch in.

The post Café des Artistes Is Returning, and Anyone Who Ever Ate There Can Help Shape It appeared first on iLovetheUpperWestSide.com.
item.content:encoded:
Photo by Team Boerum via Wikimedia Commons

Café des Artistes, the Upper West Side restaurant that closed in 2009 after more than 90 years in business, is coming back. And the team reviving it is asking anyone who ever ate, worked, or celebrated there to help shape what it becomes.

Advertisement

Café des Artistes will reopen in early 2027 at 1 West 67th Street, in the Hotel des Artistes space that housed the Leopard at des Artistes until February, according to Eater. It’ll be run by AirMax Hospitality, the group led by Ariel Arce and Max Katzenberg, whose restaurants include Tokyo Record Bar, Roscioli NYC, Pearl Box, Leonessa, and Big Pearl Caviar. The team told Eater that the Hotel des Artistes board selected the group after searching for a new operator.

Now they’re turning to the public. An ad set to run in the New York Times on Sunday, September 27, invites former diners, staff, neighbors, and anyone else with a connection to Café des Artistes to send in stories, photos, and other mementos. Submissions can also be emailed to memories@cafedesartistesnyc.com. AirMax says it’ll draw on those responses as the restaurant takes shape.

The pair first surfaced at the address in June, when Katzenberg went before Community Board 7 for a liquor license under the name Air Cafe LLC. At the time, he described a French-American-inspired, à la carte fine-dining restaurant serving lunch seven days a week starting at noon, with a last seating at 10:30 p.m. He told the committee the renovation would be purely cosmetic and that Howard Chandler Christy’s famed murals would stay untouched, adding that he’d love to track down earlier murals removed from the space decades ago and bring them back. The committee approved the application unanimously.

Both partners have roots nearby. Katzenberg told the committee he was born at the Alden on West 82nd Street and Central Park West. Arce grew up in Hell’s Kitchen and celebrated her graduation from LaGuardia High School at Café des Artistes, according to Eater. The two became business partners in 2023.

The original Café des Artistes opened in 1917 on the ground floor of the Hotel des Artistes, an apartment building built for artists, many of whose studios had no kitchens. What started as a dining room for residents eventually became a destination for performers, musicians, writers, and artists drawn to nearby Lincoln Center. Christy, an illustrator who lived in the building, began painting the restaurant’s murals of wood nymphs in 1934. The restaurant’s best-known era began in 1975, when Hungarian-born restaurateur George Lang and his wife, Jenifer, took over, serving signature dishes like salmon four ways, pot-au-feu, and tarte à l’oignon. Lang closed the restaurant in 2009, and two years later Gianfranco and Paula Sorrentino reopened the space as the Leopard at des Artistes, which ran for 15 years until closing earlier this year. The murals stayed on the walls through it all.

A chef for the new Café des Artistes hasn’t been announced yet.
